title: Sensor Filter Lab
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: Compare a moving average and a median filter on the same noisy ToF readings, with spikes and a sudden change in distance, and judge which filter is better and how window size trades smoothness against lag.

learningObjectives: Evaluate whether a moving average or a median filter is the better choice for noisy or spiky distance readings.
Explain how the window size trades smoothness (lower error) against lag (slower reaction).
Justify a filter and window choice for a robot task using measured error and lag.
prerequisites: Lists, append(), pop(), sum(), and sorted() (Chapter 5)

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.purpose: Stream a new reading every 100 ms, or pause to study the chart.

controls.label: Person walks in / Person walks away
controls.purpose: Step the true distance from 150 cm to 40 cm (or back) and measure each filter's lag.

controls.label: Window size
controls.purpose: The window parameter in the filter code.

controls.label: Noise
controls.purpose: Random noise added to each reading.

controls.label: Spike chance
controls.purpose: Chance that a reading jumps 40 to 80 cm away from the truth.

equations: raw = max(0, true + u * noise + spike), u uniform in [-1, 1]
moving average = sum(last window readings) / count
error = mean(|output - true|) over the last 100 readings
lag = readings after a step until |output - new true| <= 10 cm
assumptions: Each reading stores its random draws, so slider changes re-filter the same data.
The chart starts paused with 100 readings already filled in.
limitations: Spikes are 40 to 80 cm, much smaller than a real 8190 out-of-range reading.

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Side-by-side filter outputs on shared data with live error and lag metrics; optional streaming
keyQuestions: Why does one spike move the average but not the median?
What does a bigger window gain, and what does it cost?
Which filter would you trust to stop a robot before a wall?
commonMisconceptions: A bigger filter window is always better.
Filtering makes the robot react faster.
assessmentOpportunities: Compare average and median error at 15% spike chance.
Write and defend a filter recommendation for a given robot speed.
